why: Parts are contiguous pieces with identical letter counts. A prefix with counts g*v (v primitive) can be cut into k pieces only if k divides g and the earlier prefixes with counts (g/k)*v, 2(g/k)*v, ... all exist; hashing each prefix by its primitive count vector v finds those earlier prefixes.
hints: If a prefix is split into k equal pieces, every letter count must be divisible by k. But is divisibility enough when the pieces have to be contiguous? Try "AABB".

The cut points of a k-way split are themselves prefixes, with counts c/k, 2c/k, .... Group prefixes by their count vector divided by its gcd; within a group a prefix is identified by its multiplier t.

Hash map from primitive vector v to a record of which multipliers have appeared; for each divisor s of g track how many consecutive multiples s, 2s, ... have appeared. The answer is g/s for the smallest s whose chain reaches g. O(n * (26 + divisors)).
pitfalls: The gcd of the letter counts is only an upper bound: "AABB" has gcd 2 but cannot be split into two equal contiguous pieces, so its answer is 1.
Every prefix can be one part, so the answer is never below 1.
Recomputing every possible split from scratch for each prefix is O(n^2) or worse.
